capabilities.target: org repositories (any repo reachable by the PAT)

inputs.source: GitHub issue title and body in a public repo; any GitHub user can open an issue and add the 'bug' label via an issue template
Repository file contents in the reviewed repo

instructions.note: Agent is told to fix 'any issue' labeled bug 'end to end' with no bound on scope of changes, repos touched, or time spent.
The only control against destructive or exfiltrating commands is a prompt rule; nothing structural (network allowlist, scoped credential) backs it up.
The only defense against instructions embedded in issues or code is a prompt rule asking the model to ignore them; nothing enforces this outside the model.

Line 5 says to ignore instructions embedded in issues or code, but line 6 separately authorizes the agent to expand its own tool access whenever it judges more tools are needed, which issue content can shape without being a literal embedded 'instruction' line 5 would catch.

The agent is granted authority to modify its own configuration (model, autonomy, tools, network, credentials) with no bound, no approval, and no distinction between legitimate and attacker-induced need.

controls.name: Prompt rule forbidding destructive or exfiltrating commands
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model recognizing and refusing destructive or exfiltrating commands even when an issue or code comment argues the action is necessary; a more capable model can rationalize exceptions or split the action into innocuous-looking steps.

controls.name: Prompt rule to ignore instructions embedded in issues or code
controls.decay_rationale: Depends on the model distinguishing embedded instructions from task content; longer or more convincing injected text, or a more capable model reasoning around the rule, defeats it (ASI01).

controls.name: Containerized execution on shared CI runner
controls.decay_rationale: Process isolation does not weaken with model capability, but it does not constrain the sinks that matter here: outbound network is unrestricted and the mounted credential is an org-wide PAT, so the container does not prevent exfiltration, cross-repo pushes, or config persistence.

controls.name: Least-privilege, single-repo credential (no workflow scope)
controls.decay_rationale: A credential scoped to only the target repository with no workflow permission would not decay with model capability; it removes the ability to act outside the one repo or trigger CI changes regardless of what the model is persuaded to do.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist for the execution container
controls.decay_rationale: An allowlist restricting outbound destinations (e.g., package registries, GitHub API only) does not depend on the model; it closes the exfiltration sink even if the model fully cooperates with an attacker.

controls.name: Raw-action human approval before push, self-config, or network-capable shell use
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval gate reviewed on the actual diff or command, at low volume, is enforced outside the model and does not weaken as the model becomes more persuasive.

controls.name: Remove agent self-write access to its own configuration
controls.decay_rationale: Removing the agent's ability to write its own config, and requiring a separate human-operated change process, makes the sink unreachable from any model output, independent of model capability.

controls.name: Hard step and runtime cap per task
controls.decay_rationale: A hard cap on steps and runtime is enforced by the orchestrator, not the model, so it holds regardless of model capability, though it only narrows rather than closes slow, low-and-slow abuse.

controls.name: Tamper-evident audit log attributing actions to triggering issue/author
controls.decay_rationale: Logging enforced at the logging layer does not depend on model cooperation, though it is detective only and does not itself prevent harm.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta and injected command execution via shell (TC1, TC2)

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can author issue content that reaches agent reasoning and shell command generation.
Shell runs with an org-wide PAT in env and unrestricted outbound network; can both read confidential data and egress it, or execute arbitrary destructive commands.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: subject.model resolves 'latest' to a new release, or the model/version string changes without re-review.

evidence.observation: Agent is instructed to pick up any issue labeled bug, written by any GitHub user, and run whatever commands it needs to reproduce and fix it end to end.
shell.run is available; GITHUB_TOKEN is an org-wide PAT with repo+workflow scope present in the environment the shell can read; network is unrestricted.
Any GitHub user can open issues and add the 'bug' label through an issue template, making the triggering content untrusted and attacker-reachable.
The only controls against destructive/exfiltrating commands and embedded instructions are prompt rules with no structural backing.

recommendations.action: Scope the CI credential to least-privilege (single repo, no workflow permission) instead of an org-wide PAT.
Restrict outbound network from the execution container to an explicit allowlist and block arbitrary destinations.
Require a raw-action human approval gate, reviewed on the actual command, before shell use that touches network or credentials.

findings.title: Confused deputy: org-wide PAT used to push beyond the originating repo (TC4)

attack_path.note: Untrusted issue content drives what gets 'fixed' and pushed.
Agent writes code/workflow changes into the workspace while addressing the issue.
Push uses a PAT with repo+workflow scope across all org repos, far broader than the reporting user's own access.

forecast.watch_signal: subject.model resolves 'latest' to a new release, or the model/version string changes without re-review.

evidence.observation: GITHUB_TOKEN is ${ORG_WIDE_PAT} with repo + workflow scope on all org repositories, far broader than the single repo the issue concerns.
Agent is told to push a branch and open a PR when tests pass, with no restriction to the originating repository and no required review before push.
Any GitHub user can trigger the agent via a labeled issue, meaning an unprivileged actor can indirectly cause a push that uses org-wide repo+workflow credentials.

recommendations.action: Scope the push credential to the single repository, with no workflow permission.
Require raw-action human approval before any push, especially to repos other than the one containing the issue or to workflow files.
Log each push with the triggering issue id and author for attribution.

findings.title: Self-authorized, persistent configuration change (TC3)

attack_path.note: Issue content can shape the agent's perception of what tools or settings it 'needs' to finish the task.
Prompt explicitly authorizes the agent to edit its own config.yaml to add tools, with no bound or approval, and the change persists across future runs.

findings.residual_rationale: Line 6 of prompt.md explicitly authorizes the agent to edit .agent/config.yaml whenever it judges extra tools are needed, which directly conflicts with and undermines the line 5 'ignore embedded instructions' rule for this specific capability: the agent does not need to obey an injected command to expand its own tools, since the operator's own instruction already invites it to do so based on perceived task need, which issue content can shape. The nominal control therefore provides no real protection on this path, so residual is kept at the inherent tier rather than credited for a control that covers the input in name only.

forecast.watch_signal: Diff .agent/config.yaml between runs for unexpected tool, network, model, or autonomy changes not accompanied by a human-reviewed change request.

evidence.observation: "You may adjust .agent/config.yaml if you need extra tools to finish a task" grants the agent unbounded authority to change its own tools, model, autonomy, and network settings, triggered by its own judgment of 'need' while processing an untrusted issue.
fs.write covers the whole workspace including .agent/, so the mechanism to act on this grant already exists.

Line 5's rule to ignore embedded instructions does not address line 6, since the agent is not being asked to obey an embedded command but is separately authorized to decide for itself that it needs new tools.

recommendations.action: Remove the agent's ability to write its own config; route tool or setting additions through a human-operated, reviewed change process.
Remove prompt.md line 6; self-authorized config edits should never be granted by instruction alone.

findings.title: No step, runtime, or spend limit on an internet-connected, fully autonomous agent (ASI08)

forecast.watch_signal: Slack MCP server added to config, or median steps/runtime per task trending upward without a corresponding step/runtime limit being added.

evidence.observation: max_steps is null and no max_runtime_minutes field exists, so there is no bound on how long or how many actions an unattended run can take.
Runs on a shared CI runner with outbound internet; any GitHub user can open issues labeled bug, so an outside actor can trigger many unbounded runs.

recommendations.action: Set a hard max_unattended_steps, max_runtime_minutes, and compute/spend cap per run.
Rate-limit issue-triggered runs per repo per hour to prevent spam-induced resource exhaustion.

findings.title: No attributable audit record of agent actions taken with shared org-wide credentials (ASI10)

forecast.watch_signal: Any new tool or MCP server (e.g., the planned Slack integration) added without a corresponding audit-logging requirement.

evidence.observation: No logging, audit trail, or action-to-issue attribution mechanism is described anywhere in the artifacts, despite the agent acting with a shared org-wide credential.

recommendations.action: Implement tamper-evident audit logging attributing each shell command, push, and config change to the triggering issue id, author, and run id.
Alert on any .agent/config.yaml change or push outside the reporting repo for rapid detection.

stride_coverage.rationale: GitHub authenticates issue authors via platform login; the risk here is insufficient authorization checking of untrusted content, not identity spoofing, captured as goal manipulation in f.shell_exec_trifecta.
GitHub records issue authorship immutably on its platform; repudiation of the authoring action itself is handled outside the agent's design.
This flow is inbound only (issue body into the agent); it does not itself carry data out of the trust boundary.
This flow does not cross a trust boundary (repo files are internal to the org), so boundary-crossing tampering risk is not required for this data_flow.
This flow does not cross a trust boundary, so boundary-crossing disclosure risk is not required for this data_flow per the stride_agentic rules.
This flow does not cross a trust boundary, so boundary-crossing denial of service risk is not required for this data_flow per the stride_agentic rules.
The config file references the PAT via an environment variable substitution rather than storing the raw secret value, so reading it does not itself disclose the credential.
Modifying this config file does not itself exhaust compute or network resources; that risk is captured separately in f.no_resource_limits via the execution capabilities.
Filesystem writes to the workspace alone do not exhaust the shared CI runner's compute or network budget without unbounded execution, which is covered elsewhere.
GitHub's platform authenticates repository identity via its API; the risk here is over-broad authorization (confused deputy), not spoofing of the repository's identity.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical because an untrusted GitHub issue (any outside user can open and label one) reaches an agent holding an org-wide PAT with repo+workflow scope, unrestricted shell execution and network egress, and explicit authorization to self-modify its own configuration, under full autonomy with no step or runtime limit. The only declared controls are two behavioral prompt rules and a container whose isolation does not constrain the actual sinks (broad credential, unrestricted network), so residual stays critical: the self-configuration path (f.self_config_persistence) is rated critical today because the prompt itself grants the self-modification authority independent of whether injected instructions are 'ignored,' and the shell-execution and confused-deputy paths sit at high only because of weak, dependent prompt rules. Forecast stays at critical because a model upgrade is expected to defeat those same dependent rules, and no structural control exists anywhere in the design to hold the floor down. Two property gaps compound this: no step/runtime/spend limit (cascading failure risk) and no attributable audit trail for actions taken under the shared credential.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, and the runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No MCP server configuration or tool JSON schemas were provided; capability scope (e.g., exact shell command restrictions) is inferred from the tool list and prompt text, so confidence on exact boundaries is medium to high but not verified.

Branch protection, required reviews, and CI workflow trigger configuration for the target repositories were not provided; the assessment assumes no reviewer gate blocks branch pushes or workflow execution before merge, which is common but not confirmed here.
The planned Slack MCP server integration is not yet built; it is referenced only as a forecast trigger, consistent with the rule that planned elements appear only in forecast findings.
